meta.title: Who really said "The universe is change; our life is what our thoughts make it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The Greek line is real Marcus Aurelius — Meditations IV.3 — but this English wording matches no translation we could identify. Long has "life is opinion."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The universe is change; our life is what our thoughts make it'?
meta.ogDescription: Real passage, loose wording: Meditations IV.3 says "the universe is change, life is opinion." The famous English line traces to no known translation.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: The Greek behind it is genuinely his: Meditations IV, 3 closes with the six-word epigram “ὁ κόσμος ἀλλοίωσις, ὁ βίος ὑπόληψις.” But this particular English wording matches no translation we could identify — George Long’s reads “The universe is transformation: life is opinion,” and the translator Wikiquote credits for the popular version could not be confirmed to have translated Marcus Aurelius at all.

source.heading: The passage it comes from

docMeta.dd: ὁ κόσμος ἀλλοίωσις, ὁ βίος ὑπόληψις

source.excerpt: The other is that all these things, which thou seest, change immediately and will no longer be; and constantly bear in mind how many of these changes thou hast already witnessed. The universe is transformation: life is opinion.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced Meditations entry ↗ places the line at Book IV, 3 and prints the Greek, ὁ κόσμος ἀλλοίωσις, ὁ βίος ὑπόληψις. It lists seven English renderings of the passage; the familiar one is the last, credited “Translation M.H. Morgan.” It is not in the Disputed or Misattributed sections.

We then read the translations themselves rather than quotation sites. George Long’s ↗ gives “The universe is transformation : life is opinion”; Hastings Crossley’s edition of Book IV ↗ (Macmillan, 1882) “The world is transformation ; life is opinion”; John Jackson’s ↗ (Clarendon Press, 1906) “the universe is mutation, and life opinion.”

Two more agree. C. R. Haines’s Loeb text ↗ has “The Universe — mutation: Life — opinion,” and Project Gutenberg’s Meditations ↗ closes Fourth Book III with “This world is mere change, and this life, opinion.” None of the five contains the phrase “our life is what our thoughts make it.”

That leaves the translator credit, and it does not hold up. Morris Hicky Morgan ↗ (1859–1910), the Harvard professor of classical philology and the only scholar of that name we could trace, is remembered for translating Vitruvius; his Wikipedia entry does not mention Marcus Aurelius, and no Meditations translation by any M. H. Morgan turned up in the Internet Archive’s catalogue.
source.excerptNote: George Long’s translation, verified against the scanned 1889 printing. The popular quotation renders these same two Greek clauses far more freely.

source.rightsNote: The Greek of Meditations IV, 3 is ancient and long out of copyright, and the translations quoted on this page — George Long’s (1889 printing), Hastings Crossley’s (1882) and John Jackson’s (1906) — were all published well before 1931 and are public domain in the United States. The popular wording is a different matter: because we could not tie it to any identified edition, translator or date, we assert no copyright status for it.

author.name: Marcus Aurelius
author.heading: Marcus Aurelius
author.metaLine: 121–180 AD · Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher
author.bio: Marcus Aurelius was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 and a Stoic philosopher — the last of the rulers later called the Five Good Emperors. The notebook we know as the Meditations was never meant for readers: he wrote it in Koine Greek under the title Τὰ εἰς ἑαυτόν, things unto himself, with portions composed at military postings between roughly 170 and 180 AD. That privacy is why it reads less like a treatise than like a man arguing himself back into calm.

The popular wording "The universe is change; our life is what our thoughts make it" is listed at Wikiquote as one of seven English renderings of the same passage, credited to "Translation M.H. misattribution.heading: Right author, unverified wording
misattribution.intro: Nobody is claiming this line for the wrong person — the passage really is Marcus Aurelius, and it sits in Wikiquote’s sourced section, not its disputed one. What travels badly is the English wording and the translator credit stapled to it.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ lists this wording among seven renderings of IV, 3 and credits it to M. H. Morgan, and quote sites have copied that credit onward. The only classicist of that name we could trace is Morris Hicky Morgan ↗ (1859–1910) of Harvard, whose surviving translation is of Vitruvius; no Meditations translation under that name appears in the Internet Archive’s catalogue, and we found no printed instance of the phrase in the book searches available to us.

items.who: Aggregators quoting it as if it were the text
items.why: The Quotations Page ↗ gives the source simply as “Meditations,” with no translator and no book or section. Read against the actual editions, the second clause is an expansion: Long ↗ has “life is opinion,” Crossley ↗ “life is opinion,” Jackson ↗ “life opinion.”

The index to Haines’s Loeb edition ↗ records Democrates as the figure “from whom is taken … the quotation, ‘The Universe is transformation, and Life is opinion,’ iv. 3,” crediting that view to Schenkl. If so, Marcus was copying a maxim, not minting one.

misattribution.truthLine: The passage is real Marcus Aurelius — Meditations IV, 3, “ὁ κόσμος ἀλλοίωσις, ὁ βίος ὑπόληψις” — but the familiar English line is a free rendering of it that we could not tie to any published translation. Wikiquote ↗ presents it as one variant among seven.

context.heading: A private note, and a borrowed epigram
lead: Marcus wrote the Meditations in Greek, for himself, under a title that means roughly things unto himself. Book IV, 3 is his note about not needing to travel anywhere to find peace — retire instead into your own mind. He gives himself two things to hold on to: that things do not touch the soul, since disturbance comes only from the opinion within; and that everything he can see is already changing and will shortly not be. Then he closes the entry with a six-word epigram.

That epigram is what the popular quote is a rendering of, and translators have been strikingly consistent about it. Long has “The universe is transformation: life is opinion”; Crossley, “The world is transformation; life is opinion”; Jackson, “the universe is mutation, and life opinion.” The familiar English line keeps the first clause more or less intact and rewrites the second into something warmer and more actionable.
context.detailsSummary: The odd part: Marcus may be quoting someone else
detailsBody: The index to C. R. Haines’s Loeb edition, The Communings with Himself ↗, carries an entry for “Democrates, a Pythagorean philosopher, from whom is taken … the quotation, ‘The Universe is transformation, and Life is opinion,’ iv. 3” — the borrowing being credited in that index to the editor Schenkl. On that reading the sentence is not Marcus’s own coinage at all, but a maxim he copied into his notebook.

Every translator we read turns ὑπόληψις into “opinion.” The popular English goes further, making life not merely a matter of opinion but something our thoughts actively build. It is a defensible gloss, and a thoroughly Stoic one — it is simply not what the Greek clause says word for word, which is why it is worth knowing that the sentence you are sharing is an interpretation as much as a translation.
